question: What are the Islamic rules of mourning, and must a widow spend her idda in her husband's home?
asked: My father passed away during this crisis. What are the Islamic rulings for mourning and the etiquettes of death, especially for a widow? Is my mother allowed to leave her house and move in with me, or must she stay in the house where she lived with my father, even though nobody else is there now?
answer:
Before we get to the fiqh or the legal aspect, I think it's also important for us to give some generic advice, because subhanAllah, so many people, especially in this crisis, are passing away. And not only this, but when a person passes away, generally speaking, the family has not prepared; the family does not know what to do. And this is a knowledge that is essential and necessary for every single Muslim, and unfortunately all too often we don't study or learn, and then when it happens we don't know what to do. And so I'll take this small mini question as an opportunity to remind ourselves of some of the aspects that we need to do when somebody passes away. And by the way, if somebody you know has had a relative pass away, you can forward them this link as well, so that inshallah they can get some idea of what our religion says.

Obviously there are faith-based, iman-based aspects as well, and the most important of these is what is called in Arabic ar-rida bi-qadarillah: acceptance of the qadr of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, sabr and being patient. And acceptance here, what does it mean when we say we accept the qadr of Allah? What it means is that we acknowledge that death is inevitable. We acknowledge that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has decreed it. We acknowledge that He is the Rabb and He has the right to decree, and I don't have the right to intervene. We might not understand the wisdom of Allah, but we need to trust the wisdom of Allah. Not understanding is permissible, but not trusting is not permissible. We must trust the decision. We must trust the judgment even if we don't understand. Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows and we do not know.

And of the essence of faith is to submit to the qadr of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Allah says in the Qur'an: none can ask Allah what He does; rather, we will be asked about what we do. So when somebody passes away, there must be a level of inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un: to Allah we belong and to Him we shall return.

There's obviously not a problem to cry, to feel sad. This is something that is absolutely normal. And in fact, our Prophet ﷺ, his son Ibrahim passed away, and he was crying in front of the Sahaba. And they said, "Ya Rasulullah, do you cry?" And he said, "Yes, crying is a mercy that Allah places in the hearts of the believers." And when he visited the qabr of his mother Amina, when he visited the grave of his mother, he cried so much that he was sobbing in front of the grave, and the Sahaba, out of love for him, began sobbing as well. And they said his beard became wet with his tears.

So being accepting of Allah's qadr does not mean you're not going to be sad. Nobody is happy at the death of a loved one. What it means is that psychologically you understand that this life was not mine to own. It is Allah's life. The life that Allah 'azza wa jall blessed in this world, Allah has the right to take it away, and Allah chooses when to take it away. No soul shall die except by Allah's permission; it is something that is predetermined in a book. Nothing that you could have done or didn't do, nothing that you should have done or didn't do: nothing can change the time that Allah's qadr had come in. Allah 'azza wa jall has predetermined the qadr, the time of death, of every single one of us.

And so what qadr, what rida, what acceptance means is that at some level we will understand and we will accept that Allah has the right to do as He pleases. If somebody is hurt, if somebody is grieved, if somebody is crying, if somebody is sad, this is the essence of rahmah and compassion. There is nothing whatsoever un-Islamic. In fact, it is natural. And if somebody does not demonstrate that, then perhaps something is not regular in this situation, because to feel sad and grief is a part of Islam. Our Prophet ﷺ said when Ibrahim passed away, "We are saddened, O Ibrahim, at your loss, but we shall only say what Allah is pleased with: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un."

And always remember this hadith, which is in Sahih Bukhari: once the Prophet ﷺ passed by a lady who was sitting at a graveyard, and she was crying. And the Prophet ﷺ said to her, "Be conscious of Allah and be patient. Be patient." He's trying to give her words of encouragement, trying to console her. And she was so grieved and so distressed, she said, "Get away from me. You do not know the calamity that has befallen me." She didn't recognize him because she was grieved. And so the Prophet ﷺ continued walking away. Somebody came up to her and said, "Do you not know who he was? He was the Prophet ﷺ." And so she stood up and she rushed to the gathering. And the report says it was as if she herself had died, when she realized whom she had said that to. So she came up to the Prophet ﷺ and she said, "O Messenger of Allah, I'm so sorry, I didn't recognize you." So she's trying to excuse herself.

And of course, the Prophet ﷺ forgave her, but he gave a phrase here, and I want every one of you to remember this phrase, memorize it. What did our Prophet ﷺ say? Innama as-sabru 'inda as-sadmati al-ula: truly, patience is manifested at the first stroke of a calamity. When can you really tell that you're patient? How and when is patience manifested? The day after somebody passes away, a week after your loved one passes away, a year after your parent passes away, you can demonstrate patience; everybody does. But as soon as you hear the news, what happens in the immediate aftermath, when the shock, when the emotions are still raw? If you can maintain sabr at that point in time, then you have demonstrated to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala that you have truly believed in Allah's qadr.

And again, what is sabr? Sabr means you act in a dignified manner, in a theologically conscious manner. Sabr means that you control your limbs, you control doing things that are un-Islamic. And there are many things that are un-Islamic. Of them is wailing out loud. And what is wailing out loud? Wailing is not crying with a voice. No, that's not that. You can cry with a voice. You can cry. Some people sob. The Prophet ﷺ himself was sobbing when he was in front of the qabr of his mother Amina. When we read in the hadith that Islam forbids wailing, wailing means to raise your voice with phrases that are theologically highly problematic. For example, the phrase: "How am I going to live after you? I will not be able to survive. We have no hope without you." It is as if you are creating a God-like figure in the person that has passed away. What do you mean, how are you going to live after this person? He didn't take care of you; Allah did. Allah took care of him and you. So the One who took care of you when this person was alive will continue to take care of you when your loved one has passed away. So wailing means to say theologically indecent things that go against Allah 'azza wa jall being the Rabb.

Also, of the things that some traditions still do to this day, some religions other than Islam: when somebody passes away, they tear something of their garment to demonstrate that they are sad, and they wear torn garments for maybe a week or two. And the Shari'ah came and forbade that. It is not allowed to tear our garments. Also, in some traditions they shave the head, or they even pull out their hair, or they may go bald, obviously in other traditions other than Islam. And in our tradition, we're not allowed to do that. We're not allowed to go to that level. And the point is that we don't do things that are of an undignified nature, like flailing around and breaking things and yelling and screaming. This is not befitting the dignity of a Muslim. Death is an inevitable reality. No matter how painful it is, deep down inside there must be: okay, Allah knows best.

And again, I keep on reiterating: a natural sadness, being overcome with grief, is totally permissible; it's a sign of being human. Versus acting in an unbecoming manner: that is what is not allowed. Our Prophet ﷺ was standing in the masjid when Jibreel came and told him that Zayd ibn Haritha... Remember the adopted son story, Zayd's story: the Prophet ﷺ initially adopted him, and then Islam came and forbade that type of adoption, what is called tabanni. And there was obviously a great love. When Zayd ibn Haritha was killed in the Battle of Mu'tah, Jibreel came and informed the Prophet ﷺ. Aisha said, "I saw him from my room, I saw him in the masjid, and grief overtook him and he had to sit down." SubhanAllah, can you imagine how much the grief was, that he had to sit down? So it's not a problem to demonstrate your sadness; all of this is of the permissible issues.

Also, we have to learn the du'a for when somebody passes away, the du'a of any tragedy, not just somebody passing away. Umm Salama said that the Prophet ﷺ said that anytime a Muslim is afflicted with a tragedy and then he says, "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. O Allah, reward me in this calamity, and substitute for me something better than this calamity," Umm Salama said, anytime somebody says this, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala will substitute something better than that calamity. So whatever disaster happens to you, whatever pain happens to you, remember this du'a. And insha'Allah you will get more happiness in the near future than the pain that was caused, and Allah will bring about a joy that is bigger than the grief that was caused because of this loss. So memorize this:

> إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ، اللَّهُمَّ أْجُرْنِي فِي مُصِيبَتِي وَأَخْلِفْ لِي خَيْرًا مِنْهَا

So this is a du'a that we should all memorize as well, for when somebody passes away, and for any tragedy actually.

Also, of the things that we should do when somebody of our extended family, or even of our friends, passes away is that we should console the bereaved. This is called ta'ziyat al-mayyit in Arabic: to console the family of the one who has passed away. And the ta'ziyah is obviously proportional to the strength of our relationship with the family of the person who passed away. Obviously ta'ziyah to a brother's family is much stronger than to an acquaintance, for example, but each one has a haqq over us. And it is a part of our Sunnah to give condolences and to give ta'ziyah.

And if we have that relationship, we should even visit the family of the deceased. Our Prophet ﷺ, when his cousin Ja'far passed away, visited the house of Ja'far, and he spoke to the widow of Ja'far, and he calmed her down and he encouraged her. And he took the children of Ja'far, who were now orphans, and he hugged them and he put his hand over their heads and he made du'a for them. So he himself visited the house of his cousin Ja'far, who died as a shaheed in the same battle as Zayd, and he consoled them. And this shows us that it is Sunnah to visit the houses of the deceased, especially if they are close relatives.

Now, a point here that you should just be aware of: some of the madhhabs have expressed a minor disapproval of prolonging this visit or sitting down. They say al-julus 'ind at-ta'ziyah, and the point here is making it something that is a ritual. And you even have a handful of scholars, and even some of the Sahaba, who said that this might be a type of innovation, because it resembles some of the practices of other faith traditions. However, there are other positions as well. And of the opinions is that the overall concept of visiting the family of the deceased is permissible, as long as the culture and the context make it permissible.

So again, you need to understand that in other faith traditions there were certain rituals that would take place when foreigners came into the house, when strangers, I mean, when non-family came. And it is as if some of the early Sahaba didn't want to return to that paganistic issue. But other scholars, like Ibn Hajar, like Ibn Qayyim, said that those traditions that seem to dislike or disapprove of sitting in the house of the deceased, it is because of those pagan practices. And if those pagan practices are unknown and not being commemorated, then inshaAllah ta'ala there's no problem, just in the culturally normal manner.

This varies from culture to culture. In some cultures, if you're a close relative, you will sit there the whole day, and if you're a distant friend, you will just go for five minutes and go. It depends on culture to culture. And this, inshaAllah ta'ala, is the correct opinion: that we should not make a bigger deal about this. Your cultures, wherever you are in the world, have a certain procedure, a methodology of how you visit the family of the deceased. And as long as there are no rituals being done in there that are un-Islamic, inshaAllah ta'ala, just visit the house and express condolences.

Now, how are condolences expressed? A number of things. First and foremost, you mention the deceased in a good way. Our Prophet ﷺ said that once a person passes away, only good should be mentioned of the person. Don't mention anything bad; only mention good things. And make du'a for the deceased as well. And you can also, and you should, make du'a for the living, that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala gives them patience and sabr and increases their ajr. So of the du'as of the Prophet ﷺ, speaking to a woman in this hadith, is A'zam Allahu ajraki: may Allah increase your ajr, may Allah give you more reward for the patience that you're displaying at the death of a loved one. And you can also make generic du'a: may Allah grant him a place in Jannah, may Allah make his grave a vast place.

The point of the visit should be to demonstrate that the loss that you're suffering, I also feel it, and I'm here for you, whatever I can do. So this is a part of our religion. It is what our Prophet ﷺ did as well when he visited the house of Ja'far. Also, he himself ordered that food be gifted to the house of Ja'far. He told our mothers, he told his wives, "Prepare some food and send it to the house of Ja'far, because they are busy right now." They're not going to be cooking food.

So especially the close family and friends, and you know who you are in this case. Obviously, if you're an acquaintance, it's not the same thing. But if you're close family and friends and somebody has passed away, let's say your cousin has passed away, your uncle's family or somebody, obviously that immediate family is in great tragedy. The last thing on their minds is going to be the daily chores and routines. So you should take charge and do whatever you can: if some bills need to be paid, if some grocery shopping needs to be done, something that you know they're going to need, give some food to them. This is also a part of our religion, and our Prophet ﷺ did that as well.

And of course, when it comes to the theological issues as well, of the things that should be done is to do good deeds on behalf of the deceased. I've given an entire lecture, the final lecture I gave in the Barzakh series, you can look it up, and in that I discussed the issue of reciting Qur'an for the dead and the controversy over that, so you can go back to that lecture. But overall, the concept of gifting good deeds to the dead is something that is authentically narrated from the Sunnah. Which good deeds, and how and when, you can go back to that lecture; I went into it in more detail.

Now, all of this is the adab aspect. Let's now get to the legal aspect: the specific legal issues about what is to be done when somebody passes away and the wife is left behind after her husband passes away. And this in Arabic is called the period of hidad. And this is different than the idda, by the way, meaning that the hidad is a type of idda. Idda takes place at multiple times; idda takes place when a divorce occurs, and other things. We're not talking about those iddas today. Today we're talking about the idda that takes place when the husband dies and the wife remains alive, so she becomes a widow. So the widow's idda is called hidad. It's a special type of idda. This is the one we're talking about. There are other types of idda; that's not the topic of today.

And this concept of hidad is mentioned in the Qur'an explicitly. In Surah Al-Baqarah, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says in verse 24: those who die and leave behind their wives, Allah 'azza wa jall says, they should wait concerning themselves four months and ten days. This is very explicit in the Qur'an. Those of you who die and leave behind their wives, their wives must wait four months and ten days. This is explicit in the Qur'an, that they must wait. What does it mean that they must wait? This is the hidad period.

And there is the hadith in Sahih Muslim as well, that the Prophet said that no lady should perform hidad (I will explain what it is), no lady should perform hidad over any person who dies for more than three days, except for her husband. For her husband, she will perform it for four months and ten days. During this time, and this is the hadith, she should not wear dyed garments, except for simple garments. She should not put on kuhl, which is the antimony that is used for the eye. And she should not put on any perfume, except that when she does her ghusl after the monthly cycle, she may use, and then the Prophet ﷺ said, the basic types of perfume that were used at that point. You can call it the basic soaps that were used at that time.

Now, this hadith is very explicit. What is it saying? It is saying no person, no lady in particular. And that is because men did not do hidad, because men have to go to their daily routine and move on. They're not the ones that typically go into a state of mourning. It is the women that used to do it in the days of Jahiliyyah, and Islam allowed them to do certain things; it restricted and allowed in a certain manner. So hidad is not done by men. Hidad is permitted for women: permitted, as we're going to mention, in some cases, and wajib in other cases.

So what is hidad? Hidad is that a woman leaves the extra beautification that she would typically do, of wearing nicer garments, of wearing her makeup, of putting on her perfume. And so she abandons the better luxuries of life in order to demonstrate grief visibly in her lifestyle. Now, in the days of Jahiliyyah, hidad was done by all the women of the household for a long period of time. And by the way, to this day, certain cultures and certain faith traditions, including the Ahl al-Kitab faith tradition that has a lot of laws, also have very strict laws to this day about what women cannot do and whatnot. So our Shari'ah came and lifted a lot of these legislations.

And what it said was the following. If a person passes away who is related to a lady and is not her husband, so her father, her brother, if anybody passes away in the lady's household that is not her husband, she may choose to demonstrate her sadness and grief and to sort of abandon the niceties or the luxuries of lifestyle for three days. She might be in shock for a while, so she's not going to take care of herself that well; she'll just wear the simplest garments and whatnot. But after three days, she has to just force herself: "That's it, I'm going to get out of this. I'm going to now get back to the normal routine."

And it is authentically narrated that one of the wives of our Prophet lost a brother of hers; this is after the Prophet ﷺ passed away. And then on the fourth day after the death of her brother, she called for some kuhl and perfume to be put on. And she said, "I have no desire to do this. I don't want to," meaning, I'm so sad at the loss of my brother, "but our Prophet ﷺ said it is not allowed to perform hidad for more than three days." So I am basically forcing myself to get back in.

And this, subhanAllah, is a good psychological blessing from our religion: that for three days a lady is allowed to just absorb the shock, take some time. But on the fourth day, she just needs to collect her wits, with whatever power she's able, call upon Allah and make du'a to Allah, "Let's just move on from now on," and kind of force herself to get back into the game, because there's no point just living in that bubble of anger or hurt or depression. What's that going to do? So that's why the Shari'ah allows that grace period of three days.

Now, this is an option; it is not obligatory. Neither is it recommended, nor is it makruh; it's just there, it's completely neutral. If a lady wishes to opt in and she wants to just let that shock take its toll on her, no problem: for three days, eating minimally and just wearing the simplest garments and not really taking care of her hygiene, you know what, three days, okay. But after the third day, she needs to just get out of that phase and force herself, by Allah's blessings and Allah's power, to get back in. So this is the option. Now again, those three days are neither obligatory, nor necessarily recommended, nor makruh. It is just an option. If she is able to maintain her lifestyle completely, no problem with that at all. Now, this is for any relative other than the husband.

Okay, what if the husband passes away? This is where we get to the special ruling, which is well known in our religion and our culture as well, and that is the idda of the widow. This is called the hidad of the widowed lady. So in this case, as we said, it is not three days; it is four months and ten days. **And in this case, it is not something that is permissible; it is something that is obligatory, meaning it is wajib in the generic sense.** And again, the issue comes here: wajib has different levels. So praying five times a day is wajib, okay? And observing the hidad is wajib. But the level of wujub is nowhere near the issue of the five prayers. But it is still something that needs to be done, and it needs to be observed.

Now, here we get a lot of questions from our brothers and sisters, especially our sisters: why is this done? After all, there's no hidad for the man. What is the wisdom behind the hidad of the ladies? I have answered this question generically in multiple fatwas, and my personal philosophy is that it is a mistake to emphasize the wisdoms. Why? Because the goal of the Shari'ah in this case might not be known to us, it might not be understood, but it still must be done even if we don't understand the wisdom. In other words, suppose that I say there's a wisdom that is such and such, and a lady says, "Well, okay, but it doesn't apply to me." Will the ruling apply, yes or no? It will apply. So then what is the point of saying the wisdom is this and that, when we don't know? Allah did not specify a wisdom. And of course, at the end of the day, we simply do it to please Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, because this is what Allah has told us to do.

Now, some have said that this is to honor the marriage contract, the rights of the husband: that there's so much that the husband has done, and so this is to repay that kindness back. And of course, what if somebody were to come and flip it around and say, "Well, okay, how about if the wife did a lot for her husband? He doesn't have to do the same thing." And I don't have an answer to that. So again, this is the problem of bringing up the wisdoms: a lot of times wisdoms can easily have holes poked in them, and there's not much to be said about that.

Another thing that can be said in this regard, and some people have said this, is the issue of what if she's carrying a child. And this is a very valid point: we want to make sure, because obviously the man is not an issue if he marries soon after that, but if a lady marries and she's pregnant from the first husband, that would be very, very awkward. But then the response can be: why four months and ten days? And I don't have a reason, because these days you can discover pregnancy with one test. So these are all wisdoms.

One of my teachers gave a wisdom as well, but again, it's a general wisdom, Allah knows best: that generally speaking, the woman is the one that suffers more of the harshness of the man than the other way around. Generally speaking, it is the man who might say something or do something that he shouldn't have done. And when the lady is in her house, her husband's house, for four months and ten days, it is at that point in time that she not only thinks of the bad, she will also remember the good. One of my teachers said this: during this timeframe, insha'Allah ta'ala, the good of the man will be much more than the bad, so she will ask forgiveness for the man if he has done something he should not have done. This timeframe also allows the lady to reminisce about the good times, about the kindness, and to then ask Allah's forgiveness for the man.

At the end of the day, dear sisters and brothers, these are all wisdoms that are coming from the minds of people. We don't know the wisdom. And even if we don't understand it, it is very explicit in the Qur'an, and it is very clear in the hadith as well: four months and ten days.

Now, what is to be avoided in these four months and ten days? A number of things. The hadith mentions the main ones. Number one, decorative garments. Now, the hadith mentions dyed garments, and some scholars have been very strict, any color, but some scholars have been more reasonable. The point here is that every lady and every man has clothes that are regular and day-to-day, the worn clothes, and then they have the fancy garments. Everybody does this, right? Even the Prophet ﷺ, by the way. And so the point of the hadith is that she should not be wearing decorative garments; she should wear the most simple clothes for that timeframe, even if there's some color on it. Because these days, subhanAllah, almost every clothing item has some color on it, and in the days of the Prophet, color was a very expensive thing. So when he said masbugh, a dyed garment, the meaning here is basically the expensive garment.

And this, inshaAllah, is the correct position: that the goal here is that you wear simple clothes, whatever is the regular norm. And again, this would vary from time to place, to culture, to family, to socioeconomic status. What is simple for a very wealthy couple is not going to be the same as what is simple for a couple that is not so wealthy. But every couple, every family knows: this is the simple thing that I wear. And so during those four months and ten days, she should never wear any glamorous clothes, any glitzy outfit. She needs to be very simple.

Also, very explicitly, our Prophet said to remove the kuhl: no kuhl. And from this we also understand that any type of decorative makeup, any type of things that are applied, the mascara, all the makeups that are applied here, should be avoided. Now again, in our timeframe, this is a very complex system of makeups and whatnot. That which is just what they call touch-ups or whatnot, inshallah there's no haraj in that. But anything that is decorative, that is really meant to be beautifying above and beyond... The quick two-, three-minute routine, like some cream, some lotions, inshallah that's something that is permissible. But the whole decorative stuff that takes long periods of time, that is something that should be avoided during those four months and ten days.

Also jewelry, anything that is zinah. Now, some scholars have made an exception if it's something that she has been wearing regularly throughout her life, and others say she should try to take it off during the timeframe. But definitely she should not be dressing up in any extra jewelry during this timeframe, the four months and ten days.

Now again, these are above and beyond. She should maintain her personal hygiene. She should maintain her regular routine of showers and combing her hair and whatnot. But to go out of her way and to deck herself out, this is something that should be avoided for four months and ten days. Okay, so this is something that is very clear from the hadith.

Now, the other issue comes, the big issue here: where must she stay? And again, there's quite a lot of discussion, even amongst the Sahaba, by the way. This is a ruling where the four madhhabs had an opinion, but amongst the Sahaba we have very diverse, or very heated, if you like, two sides. And again, I'm not going to go into advanced detail here. You either ask the shaykh that you trust, or, if you're trusting the position that I have after the research that I've done and the positions that I hold, my position, the summary of it (this is not the time to go into fiqh details), is as follows.

**The default position is that the widow should live those four months and ten days in the house that she used to live in with her husband, if it is logistically feasible to do so.** The default, what you resort to as plan A, is that she should be in the house where her husband and she used to live, basically where the couple used to live, their regular residence. So for example, if they were on vacation somewhere and he passes away on vacation, she doesn't remain in the hotel for four months and ten days. She will return to the house that they used to occupy, and she will live there for four months and ten days.

However, this is the default. If there is any reasonable logistical issue, anything, not necessarily a life-and-death situation, anything that becomes a nuisance, what we call in Arabic a haraj, not necessarily difficulty to the level of darura, but something that makes life awkward or difficult: for example, if she is all alone in a city and there are no relatives and she's elderly, and she can go get some food from the neighbors, but it's a very difficult thing; nobody's going to look after her. In this case, insha'Allah ta'ala, there is no haraj, no sin, for her to move into her son's house in another city, or any place. And she stays in that location for four months and ten days and takes that as a base for the four months and ten days. And if something happens during that interim where she is forced to move to another place, so be it.

The point is that she should try. Her niyyah should be, the default should be: "I'm going to remain in the house of my marriage," or at least, the marriage here means the last place that her husband and she were living in. "And if that's not possible, then I'll move to the house of a mahram that is safe for four months and ten days." And if something needs to happen and she moves, inshaAllah, no problem there as well.

Also, it is authentically narrated from a number of companions that their daughters' husbands passed away, and they would tell their daughters to come to their houses during the daytime, and then they would send them back at night to the houses of their husbands. So what is allowed: during the daytime, she may exit the house for any legitimate need, whether she is working and has to go to work, or she's visiting her parents or whatnot; she may leave during the daytime. And then she should get to her house and spend the night in the house of her husband. That is the ruling: she is allowed to leave during the daytime for any need of hers. And this need doesn't have to be, as I said, life-threatening. Even if she's lonely, she wants to visit her daughter or something, and anxiety is increasing. But she should try her best to go back to the house where she is living for four months and ten days.

Now again, if something happens and she doesn't spend every single night there, there's no expiation or kaffarah, but she should ask Allah's forgiveness and try her best to do that. And once again, this level of strictness of staying in that house can be mitigated in case of any health issue, any age issue, any logistical issue, any psychological issue. If it's really an issue for the lady to remain alone, inshaAllah ta'ala, make alternative arrangements where they can stay. But still, the default position should be that she stays in the place of her husband's residence for four months and ten days.

And of course, this begins from the day that the husband passes away; that will be the first day. And so you go for four months and ten days. These are lunar months, not solar months. So you can count the lunar months, count them, and you can make an average of 30 days. So that's four times 30, plus 10: that's going to be 140 days. So 140 days from the date of the death of the husband. After that, all of the restrictions are lifted and she can go back to normal.

And of course, of the restrictions, the most obvious one is that marriage is not allowed, if she's a lady that is young and wants to get married again. So for that timeframe, there can be no concrete proposal, much less any nikah. The Qur'an allows for an indirect proposal. An indirect proposal is that news comes to her, somebody comes to her and basically generically says, for example, "I'm interested in getting married," and obviously this will vary from time to place. The Qur'an does not allow an explicit proposal or an explicit acceptance; this is haram. For four months and ten days, there should be a period of mourning.

But in case, for example... Sometimes a lady doesn't know what's going to happen: where am I going to go after four months and ten days? And so maybe a gentleman is wanting to get married, and he just generically says, "I'm looking for a wife, and maybe in a few weeks we'll see what is possible," and leaves it at that. Just leave a dot, dot, dot. So the hint is given. That consolation is there that, okay, inshallah, something can happen at that time. But the Shari'ah does not allow explicit marriage in this timeframe; in fact, not even an explicit proposal during this timeframe. So these are the laws of the hidad.
